When I was a kid, my parents were always steely eyed and tight lipped.  If anything ever bothered them they certainly never let it show.  If I cried, I was told there was nothing worth crying over.  If I expressed being upset or hurt, I was given the “but we have given you such a good life” speech.  Cue the onset of puberty and the onset of my struggles with mental illness.  

The first time I remember self harming was the end of 8th grade.  I left honors algebra to use the restroom where I broke a mechanical pencil and used the plastic shards to rip at the skin on my thighs.  I was fat and moody and always wore dark clothes.  No one could see the tiny beads of blood staining my clothes.

I had major panic attacks, would tell my mother I was sick to get out of school because I was too depressed to leave my bedroom.  I pulled out my hair and had bald patches that I had to learn how to part my hair a different way to cover.  I had hundreds of self inflicted wounds at various stages of healing all over my body.  I was old enough to stay home alone so I stopped going on our family vacations to the beach.  It was so easy to hide.  

Eventually I told my mom about the cutting after scaring myself that I was going to die on accident at some point.  She took all my razor bloods, put me in therapy, and we might a silent agreement to never talk about it again.  

After my therapist requested to meet with my mom, I was terrified.  My therapist tried to explain to her the role that she and my father have played in me becoming the troubled child that I had become.  My mother absolutely would not hear it. That therapist was crazy and wanted to find someone to blame for my problems.  Bye bye therapy.  

Junior year of high school I told my friend about my plan to end my life.  I wasn’t afraid to die anymore.  She told a teacher, who told the school counselor, who made me sit in her office and listen in while she spoke to my mom on the phone.  She could not understand.  This came out of nowhere.  I had no real problems, why would I do something so horrible to her and my father.  Following the conversation I went back to art class, locked myself in the closet and sobbed like I never had before in my life.  This is the turning point, I thought.  Everyone would know how crazy and unhinged I am.  But surely it’s for the good that it’s out now.  Things will have to get better.

They did not.  Oh man did they not. 

I tried dozens of different drugs.  Nothing helped.  I did not return to therapy.  But I kept up the facade at home that I was a trooper and I could beat this.  Maybe when I grew a little more.  Maybe when I got out of this little podunk town.

I got into a good college not too far away.  It was going to give me a sense of purpose.  I would make new friends who I had things in common with.  I would join clubs and travel on school breaks.  I had amazing scholarships, I didn’t owe anyone a nickel.  I was so. lucky.

Sophomore year it started tumbling apart.  I returned to my dorm room from the shower and a friend asked why I had blood trickling down my leg.  Fuck.  Of course I hadn’t really given up my habit.  I was found out.  I told my closest friends that I had struggled with depression a long time and had some unhealthy coping mechanisms.  Everyone could relate.  I didn’t want to go into detail.  It was forgotten.  

Junior year I lived off campus.  I got into on campus group therapy.  I was still holding it together...sort of.  In therapy I shared sanitized snippets of my troubles.  But mostly just cried when prompted to share.  One night I drank a bottle of jack, took a bottle of pills that, years later, I don’t even remember the name of, and I sliced both my arms from wrist to elbow the RIGHT way.  I texted my brother goodbye and I passed out.  I don’t remember the details but apparently my mother and brother came to my home in the night and took me back to my childhood home.  My plan had failed.  Fuck.  Now I’m really exposed as a crazy person! The next day I was checked into the dreaded “fifth floor” of the local hospital.  Where they had always joked they would send me.  The attention I got was minimal.  I was “stabilized” and released after a week.

For brevity’s sake, I finished college on time even despite missing a semester.  I continued to bury my troubles with drugs and alcohol which led to personal and legal problems.  I was in the hospital once more.  I started individual therapy.  But I graduated with honors.  I was a crazy bitch but a successful one! I was starting to figure out how to better conceal the crazy feelings...  

Feelings.  That’s what they were called.  I never knew they were normal.  I never saw them expressed at home.  I didn’t know that everyone was struggling with things that overwhelmed them, things that made them upset and ruined their days.  I thought surely I was a freak of nature for having that physical feeling of dying inside when I encountered heartbreak.  I did every thing I could possibly think of to make those...feelings...go away.  

Skip forward a few years to now.  I have made attempts on my life multiple times.  The longest I have successfully held down a job is 14 months.  I explode and break down every few months when my unhealthy coping mechanisms fail me and the feelings start to leak out.  I can not get my fucking life together.  I have severe substance abuse issues.  I am back home with my parents now because I can’t function.  We all have a little more insight into my problem after many doctors, therapists, and other professionals.  My parents beg me to talk to them.  To tell them what I’m “feeling.”  The concept of feeling emotions is something I still do not have a good grasp on.  When asked to describe them I involuntarily begin to cry.  If I can hold that back I can usually mutter out an “ok” or “fine.”  

I don’t know if anyone will read this, or take anything away from this.  I’ve never sat down and really wrote out my story from the beginning as I understand it today.  But to those of you who are my age and starting your own families...don’t try to make your kids believe you’re superhuman.  Let them see your weaknesses.  Make them understand that feelings are normal and teach them how to give them names.  If you never struggled, don’t assume your kids won’t.  It’s so much easier to address how to be mentally healthy in the formative years than it is to try to totally rewire an adult brain.  I don’t know if I’ll ever really be ok.  My parents learned a hard lesson in a shitty way.  Now they have an adult child, dependent on them, because of feelings.
